children: When the Reserve Bank of India established its special FCNR(B) swap facility in June, its primary objective was to attract sufficient foreign currency to increase its reserves and give the rupee some room to move. When the facility was closed at the end of August — one month earlier than scheduled — it had achieved that aim, raising $65.4 billion in new deposits and $72.8 billion when the wider range of measures was taken into account.
The scale in nominal terms was larger than in 2013, when the RBI’s two special swap windows attracted about $34 billion, with $26 billion raised through the FCNR route.

Yet the rupee, which was close to ₹95 per dollar when the scheme was launched, was still trading at about the same level several months later, reaching as high as ₹95.60 for a short time when the closure was announced.
Looking for rupee appreciation is the wrong yardstick

Even though there had been an inflow of tens of billions of dollars, the currency had not changed much. This might lead to the interpretation that the scheme had not achieved its aim. Yet this view fails to take into account the actual purpose of the FCNR(B) window and misrepresents the way in which currency markets set prices.
Mechanics of the swap

The instinct to expect appreciation is based on a straightforward explanation: money comes into the country, is exchanged for rupees, and the increased supply pushes the exchange rate up. However, the FCNR(B) scheme worked differently. Banks first took in deposits and then exchanged the dollars directly with the RBI.

The attractiveness of the scheme increased because eligible FCNR(B) deposits were excluded from both the cash reserve ratio (CRR) and the statutory liquidity ratio (SLR), which, in turn, enabled banks to make greater use of the funds they had raised.
As a result,

the central bank took a large part of that inflow on to its own balance sheet rather than allowing it to enter the open market. The purpose of the scheme was primarily to build up reserves and provide external financing, with only an indirect effect on stabilising the spot market, rather than a direct one.
Dollar demand remained strong

Above all, the rupee’s value is not based solely on inflows; it is affected by the balance between the supply of dollars and the demand for dollars. At that time, demand was particularly strong. The cost of India’s oil imports was considerable, with the price of Brent crude at around $89 per barrel in mid-August, while geopolitical tensions had kept prices high.

Pressure on the rupee came from dollar demand linked to oil, routine imports, hedging operations, weak portfolio flows and other capital-account factors. These forces likely offset the stabilising effect of the facility, resulting in a more stable currency rather than a significant appreciation.
Stability was a success
It is important to examine this stability in its own right.
The real question to ask is not how much the rupee appreciated, but by how much it would have depreciated in the absence of the scheme.

The reserve-building effect was visible in the data: India’s foreign-exchange reserves rose to approximately $707 billion by 7 August. Viewed in this way, the facility may not have delivered a stronger rupee, but it appears to have helped contain the forces pushing it lower.
Although this counterfactual cannot be directly observed, the effectiveness of the facility should be evaluated in light of the external pressures affecting the rupee.
Liquidity costs also mattered

There was also a domestic cost to consider. For each dollar that the RBI took in, rupees were injected into the banking system, increasing existing liquidity and making it more difficult to conduct monetary policy.
This helps explain why the facility was closed early.

The objective had never been to hold the dollars accumulated indefinitely; rather, it was to establish a sufficient buffer before the costs of holding additional liquidity exceeded the advantages of having extra reserves.

The fact that the facility was closed early indicates that the RBI had built up a substantial reserve and financing buffer and regarded it as unnecessary to keep the subsidised facility open indefinitely.

It is also possible that the RBI had taken into account the costs associated with liquidity and hedging resulting from accepting further inflows, although it did not publicly state that these costs were the reason for the closure.
The buffer will cushion India during the next crisis

This does not rule out the possibility of a benefit for the rupee in the future. The deposits obtained have maturities ranging from three to five years, and a stronger reserve position can lead to a lower risk premium being attached to rupee assets even before any further dollars are swapped.
Should oil prices decline, capital flows return or geopolitical tensions ease, the buffer built up this summer could translate into actual strength for the currency.

The inflow is not a permanent addition to India’s external wealth, as the associated foreign-currency liabilities will begin falling due from 2029 and extend through 2031, creating a future repayment or rollover requirement.

One of the primary achievements of the RBI this year was not to appreciate the rupee, but to make it more difficult for the currency to depreciate. If the FCNR(B) facility is assessed only on the small adjustment in the exchange rate, the essential point is overlooked: a lack of obvious change does not mean that there was no effect.
Utsav Nayak is Research Analyst, Chintan Research Foundation.)
Views are personal and do not represent the stand of this publication.

title: Rupee appreciation is not the issue, FCNR (B) inflows provide the buffer for the next crisis
